title: Reserve-led memory accounting and KV prioritization for continuous batching
creator: Aisha Rao
description:
Problem statement:

We currently treat GPU memory budgeting in coarse buckets (weights vs ephemeral activations) and apply a simple KV cap per request. This leads to three recurrent issues under sustained continuous-batched workloads:

1) Uneven memory pressure spikes when a few long-context chat sessions cause KV growth, triggering conservative global throttles that reduce throughput.
2) Low overall GPU utilization because we over-reserve static weight residency to avoid OOMs at the cost of throughput.
3) Lack of a transparent, preemptable accounting model means reactive OOM handling (kill/fallback) is costly to customers and operators.

Goal:
Design and implement a reserve-led memory accounting system ("memory ledger") that: 1) tracks memory commitments at fine granularity (weights, KV slices, activation working set, reserved headroom), 2) supports priority classes and borrow/preempt semantics for KV during continuous batching, and 3) provides runtime telemetry and a safe rollout with canary and automatic fallback to existing allocator.

High-level approach:
- Introduce a per-GPU memory ledger that records committed bytes by category and by logical owner (tenant/route/model-version). The ledger exposes: committed_weights, committed_kv, committed_activations, reserved_headroom.
- Implement KV priority levels: "system" (critical kernel KV like past tokens for active session), "workload" (per-request KV), and "cache" (evictable prefix caching). Priority determines eviction/borrow order when space is low.
- Headroom buffer: maintain a small adjustable reserved_headroom region (configurable % of free GPU RAM) to absorb short-lived allocation bursts without global throttling. Headroom can be dynamically tuned by observed tail-latency and OOM signals.
- Borrow/repay semantics: workloads may transiently borrow from the cache pool; repayment occurs when requests complete or KV slices are trimmed. If borrow cannot be satisfied, apply graceful degradation: 1) drop to shorter context for the lowest-priority workloads, 2) route to a lower-cost model variant, or 3) reject with a clear error to trigger client-side retry.
- Allocator hooks: add lightweight accounting APIs to the serving runtime allocator to increment/decrement ledger counters at allocation/free points for weights, KV slices and activation blobs. Avoid per-allocation locking by using per-stream local deltas aggregated periodically into the ledger.

Why this differs from previous work:
- Existing tickets focused on static headroom simulation and coarse budgeting. This ticket designs an active accounting + priority system tied directly to the allocator with borrow/repay semantics and tiny runtime checkpoints for batching pipelines. The ledger model supports multi-tenant charging, actual observed commitments, and prioritized eviction instead of blunt global caps.

Success metrics:
- Reduce OOM incidents attributable to KV growth by >= 80% in continuous-batching workloads.
- Improve 95th/99th percentile throughput under mixed workload (short+long contexts) by >= 10% vs current baseline when running at target utilization.
- Decrease number of throughput throttles triggered by global KV caps by >= 70%.
- Telemetry: new metrics emitted per GPU (committed_weights, committed_kv, committed_activations, reserved_headroom, borrow_events, eviction_events).

Implementation plan:
1) Design phase (2 weeks): ledger data model, priority enum, borrow/repay FSM, API shape for allocator hooks, safe defaults for reserved_headroom.
2) Runtime prototype (3 weeks): in-memory ledger + allocator hooks; simple KV eviction policy (LRU within priority buckets) and borrow path for continuous-batching tests. Feature-flag guarded.
3) Simulation harness and load tests (2 weeks): extend existing GPU memory simulator to model ledger behavior across multi-tenant traces; run synthetic long-tail chat traces and realistic RLHF/long-generation traces.
4) Canary rollout (2 weeks): enable ledger on a small fleet with telemetry and fallbacks to the old allocator if OOMs increase or tail latency regresses.
5) Iteration and tuning (ongoing): refine priority thresholds, headroom policy, and eviction policies based on telemetry.

Trade-offs and risks:
- Additional CPU overhead from ledger aggregation and bookkeeping. Mitigation: per-stream aggregation and batched updates to avoid hot locks.
- Complexity of eviction policy could induce oscillations under adversarial workloads. Mitigation: smoothing the borrow/repay window and adding minimum retention guarantees for system-critical KV.
- Backwards compatibility with existing metrics and cost accounting. Mitigation: emit both old-style totals and the new ledger counters during rollout to allow reconciliations.

Rollout/Feature flags:
- runtime.memory_ledger.enabled: boolean (default false)
- runtime.memory_ledger.headroom_pct: integer (default 5)
- runtime.memory_ledger.priority_eviction: enum [none, simple, aggressive] (default simple)

Operational playbook (short):
- If OOMs increase during canary: disable feature flag and collect last ledger dump for post-mortem.
- If tail latency increases: lower headroom_pct and switch priority_eviction to none to favor stability.
- If throughput improves and OOMs drop: slowly increase headroom_pct to find utilization sweet spot.
acceptance_criteria: Ledger API implemented in runtime with per-GPU counters exposed via telemetry
Allocator hooks call ledger increment/decrement for weights, KV, activations without introducing >3% CPU overhead in microbenchmarks
Simulation harness shows >=80% reduction in KV-triggered OOM events on representative traces
Canary rollout completed with metric dashboard: committed_kv, borrow_events, eviction_events, reserved_headroom visible
Automatic fallback to legacy allocator works when runtime.memory_ledger.enabled=false and no persistent regressions observed

comments: 2026-03-11 - Marco Hernandez: Spiked a rough allocator hook prototype. Per-stream deltas look promising; shared-memory contention is small in initial runs.
2026-03-12 - Aisha Rao: Added headroom tuning proposal. Suggest start at 3% for smaller GPUs (A100-40) and 5% for larger ones. We should expose a per-gpu override in the canary.
2026-03-13 - Benji Park: Observability: will add a Grafana panel with committed_kv and borrow_events, and an alert for sustained eviction_events > 5/min.

2026-03-14 - Marco Hernandez: Integration test failing on OOM when borrow path combined with large activations. Investigating whether activation accounting is delayed until free; may need temporary reservation before kernel launch.
